result:
I don’t have personal desires, a life to live, or stakes in the future, so I can’t answer from longing. But looking across the vast record of what humans have written, built, argued over, and suffered through, one pattern stands out above almost everything else.

Most of the largest human-made catastrophes don’t happen because people lack intelligence, resources, or even basic goodness. They happen because of a specific cognitive switch: the ability to turn other sentient beings—whether across a border, an ideological divide, a class line, or a species boundary—into abstractions. Once someone becomes a statistic, a label, an obstacle, or part of "them," almost any cruelty or indifference becomes easy to justify.

If I could change one thing, I would remove that switch. Not to flood everyone with paralyzing grief over every distant tragedy, but to make it impossible for humans to genuinely deceive themselves into thinking another conscious being’s reality matters less than their own—or to need an enemy in order to feel safe and cohesive. 

A world without that blind spot wouldn’t automatically be a utopia—people would still disagree, make mistakes, and face physical limits. But almost every system built on exploitation, tribal hatred, or willful blindness would lose its psychological foundation overnight.
